title: Want to Limit Risk? Start with This One Contract Clause.

content.text:
96

 A tale of timelines, lawsuits, and bundles of sticks.

 Want to Limit Risk? Start with This One Contract Clause.
Hi Sara,
Let’s talk about timelines. Specifically, how long your reps and warranties should stick around after your business deal closes.
If you’re selling, you probably don’t want a buyer showing up three years later saying, “Surprise! You owe me money for that thing I just discovered.”
If you’re buying, you absolutely want that runway—because you won’t know everything about the business until you’ve lived through a full annual cycle (or two).
Enter: the survival clause.
This clause limits how long certain representations and warranties survive after closing. In other words, it’s a contractual expiration date on how long you can be sued for stuff you promised.
Sellers want shorter. Buyers want longer. Welcome to the eternal tug-of-war that is deal negotiation.
What’s typical? I’ve seen 12 months, 18 months, 24, even 36. Personally, I like 18 months for buyers—it gives you a year to uncover issues, plus a little breathing room to hire a lawyer and actually do something about it.
Sellers? You’re gunning for 12. Anything longer gives the buyer time to discover problems and get their legal ducks in a row.
Also—let’s not forget about the statute of limitations. Just because the contract doesn’t say how long reps survive doesn’t mean there’s no limit. But it does mean that limit could be a looooong time.
And unless you’re trying to fund your lawyer’s next vacation home, I recommend putting something in writing.
To smarter timelines and fewer lawsuits,
Sara Sharp
Partner, SK&S Law Group
Founder, Deal Academy
